To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the insoluble micrometer-sized particles in the GISP 2 (Greenland ice sheet Project 2) ice core record reflect environmental changes in the Northern Hemisphere during the Pleistocene-Holocene transition (10 500 to about 14 000 years ago); (2) the microparticle record indicates that the Younger Dryus was a period of increased aridity, and that the warmer Preboreal period was characterized by greater storm activity; and (3)
the insoluble micrometeorite record in the GSP2 ice core reflects changes in environmental conditions during the Pleistocene-Holocene transition.
the microparticle record from the GISP2 ice core reflects the changing climate of the Younger Dry-as and Preboreal in the Northern Hemisphere.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the mechanisms that control the long-distance transport of insoluble micrometeorites (insoluble microparticles) from the Northern Hemisphere continents to the Greenland ice sheet during the Younger–Dryas–Holocene transition.
the reconstruction of the environmental conditions of the northernmost Atlantic Ocean region and Greenland from 10 000 yr ago to present.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the insoluble micrometeorological record in the GSP2 ice core reflects changes in environmental conditions associated with the expansion and contraction of the polar vortex, and that these changes are related to the strength of the zonal and meridional circulation systems in the North Atlantic region.
changes in insoluble microparticles in the GISP core reflect the changing strength of zonal winds (and associated changes in the polar vortex) and the associated changes in storminess and aridity.

the insoluble micrometeorite record in GISP2 ice reflects the changing position of the northernmost Atlantic storm track, which is in turn related to the changing position of a more expanded (contraction) polar vortex, and therefore the changing climate of the Northern Hemisphere during the Pleistocene-Holocene transition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the insoluble micrometeorite record is sensitive to both synoptic- and hemispheric-scale climate changes.

the GISP2 microparticle record is a proxy for the strength of the polar vortex, and thus a record of the strength of the northernmost Atlantic storm track and the associated aridity in the Northern Hemisphere.

the insoluble micrometeorite record in the Greenland Ice Core Project 2 ice core provides an integrated record of changes in the Northern Hemisphere atmospheric circulation during the last deglaciation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the insoluble micrometeorite record in the Gisp2 ice core can be used to track changes in the position of synoptic-scale circulation systems in the northern North Atlantic region.
microparticle data in the GISP 2 ice core can be interpreted in terms of the changing position of the polar vortex, the position of the mid-latitude storm track, and the strength of zonal winds.
the insoluble micrometeorite record in ice cores provides a proxy for changes in the strength, position, and variability of the polar vortex.
